::: {#exm-procedure-comparison}
#### Comparing the procedures in the simulated family

Each procedure was run on the same simulated family of @exm-rejection-counts
in 2000 repetitions.
The table collects the estimated FWER, FDR and power:

```{r}
#| label: procedure-comparison
#| code-fold: false
comparison <- t(sapply(sim_counts, summarize_counts))
rownames(comparison) <- c(
  "Unadjusted", "Bonferroni", "Holm", "Benjamini-Hochberg"
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 3)
```

Unadjusted testing has the highest power and no error control.
The two FWER procedures keep the FWER below 0.05 and give up most of the power;
Holm's procedure never rejects fewer hypotheses than the Bonferroni correction.
In this simulation BH has the highest power among the procedures that control an error rate,
because it only promises to control the FDR.
Its FWER is far above 0.05, which BH does not promise to control.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#rem-choosing-error-rate}
#### Choosing an error rate

Control the FWER when a single false positive is costly,
as in a confirmatory trial that tests a handful of outcomes.
Control the FDR when the rejections are leads to follow up,
as in a screen of thousands of genes,
where a small fraction of false leads is acceptable.
The choice should be made before looking at the data.
:::
